job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Jamal Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Augsburg, in the flat above my father's electrical firm, so there's usually a van outside. I'm doing a master's in embedded systems, which means mornings in lectures and afternoons in the lab writing code for a small controller board. Last summer I spent three months at a car parts supplier writing tests for firmware. My fiancée Lena, who's a dental assistant, and I are getting married next July, so a lot of my evenings go on wedding lists and quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I'd bet on. At church and in the firm I'd say you can't replace a good electrician or a careful engineer. I'd tell the lads at my dad's firm that the people shouting about it want something to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. I use AI now and then for explaining errors, and it's useful but not magic. My own worry is money: the wedding is next July, I owe about thirteen thousand, and I haven't got a job offer yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's in June, send applications to about twenty firms, and work with my dad on weekends to bring in cash. I'd keep the AI use light, only for explaining, and I'd double-check anything it tells me. I'd also keep the wedding budget tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm about technology. A bit tense about the date, because a wedding is a deadline of its own. Lena says we can scale it down, but I want to do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about the wedding if money were tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut the guest list from a hundred and twenty to eighty and book a smaller room at the parish hall. I'd rather be married on time with fewer people than late with a big party. Lena's mother would be upset, but she'd cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad offer if the job search drags?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad says I can take the apprentices' wage for a few months if the job search drags. I'm proud of that, but I'd be embarrassed too, after five years at university. I'd rather work my own field.

say: I'd say you can't replace a good **electrician** or a careful engineer.
I'd tell the lads at my dad's firm the people shouting are **selling something**.
think: I use AI now and then and it's **useful but not magic**.
My real worry is **money**: the wedding in July, thirteen thousand in loans and no offer.
do: Finish the master's and send about **twenty applications**.
Work with my dad at weekends for **cash**.
feel: I feel **calm** about technology, but tense about the wedding date.
S0.quote: I'd rather be married on time with fewer people than late with a big party.
fieldNote: Jamal's worry is **cash and timing**, not technology.
He is **proud and embarrassed** about his father's fallback offer.
His faith and family make the **wedding** a fixed point in every plan.

steps.text: Finish the embedded systems master's in June
Send about twenty applications to embedded software employers
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80
Keep the July wedding date and book the parish hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should neither panic nor cheer. I'd tell people at church that work is still honest work, but it will look different. And I'd tell the lads that the electricians will be the last to be replaced, but even they will see the paperwork go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried about my type of work. Writing tests for firmware is exactly what a tool can do, and a lot of my internship was that. I think there'll be fewer junior jobs, and I need one to start my married life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more, but with checks, and get good at reviewing what they produce. I'd apply for embedded roles where the hardware is physical and testing needs a person, like cars and machines. And I'd keep helping my dad, who's starting to quote jobs with software and needs someone to set it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit anxious, if I'm honest. I'd keep it from Lena, because she's got enough worries with the dental practice cutting hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you keep it from Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's afraid the practice will let her go. They're trying out a program that books patients and sends reminders, and it does half of what the front desk did. She'd say she's fine, and I'd see that she isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the two of you do if hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we both keep earning and cut back before July. If either of us loses hours, we'd move in with my parents for a year. It's not ideal, but it's what families do.

say: I'd say we should neither **panic nor cheer**.
I'd tell the lads that electricians will be the **last** to be replaced.
think: Writing **firmware tests** is exactly what a tool can do.
There'll be fewer **junior jobs**, and I need one to start married life.
do: Use the tools more but **check** what they produce.
Apply for embedded roles where the **hardware is physical**.
Help my dad set up **quoting software**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but I'd keep it from Lena.
S1.quote: If either of us loses hours, we'd move in with my parents for a year. It's not ideal, but it's what families do.
fieldNote: Jamal worries about **both incomes**: his and Lena's front-desk job.
He plans to use tools **with checks**, in line with his steady style.
He hides worry to **protect** his fiancée.

steps.text: Use AI tools for test writing and check every result by hand
Apply for embedded roles in cars and machines where hardware is physical
Plan to move in with my parents for a year if hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for families to plan. I'd say to people at church that we should look after one another, and ask the town council to prepare. I'd tell the lads at my dad's firm to learn the new equipment now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be afraid. The thinking jobs go in 2028, and mine is one of them. The hands-on side, like my dad's firm, lasts a few years longer, and that's where I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for my dad full time and train as an electrician, because I could take over the firm in time. I'd postpone my job search and probably the wedding, or shrink it to the family. I'd use the tools to get my dad's firm organised, because that's where they help most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be walking around the flat at night. Lena and I have been planning for two years and this would turn it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really postpone the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd do a small wedding in July with the family and a meal. A big wedding in a year like that would feel wrong. I'd rather have a quiet start than a loud party and money worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise taking over the firm with your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hardest bit. He'd say I should keep my own career. But he's sixty and tired, and the firm's customers are mostly older people who'd stay with a person they know. I think he'd say yes in the end.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** for families to plan.
I'd say we should **look after** one another at church.
think: The thinking jobs go in **2028** and mine is one of them.
The hands-on side, like my dad's firm, lasts **a few years longer**.
do: Work for my dad full time and train as an **electrician**.
Use tools to get my dad's firm **organised**.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and walk around the flat at night.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a quiet start than a loud party and money worries.
fieldNote: Jamal turns to the **family firm** as his fallback and future.
He would **shrink the wedding** before touching the date.
His **steady** style is to use tools where they help most.

steps.text: Work for my dad's electrical firm full time
Train as a qualified electrician through an evening course
Hold a small family wedding in July instead of a big one
Set up quoting and scheduling software for my dad's firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if we're sensible. At church I'd say teach the young a trade as well as a degree. At work I'd say it's time to learn the tools properly, once they've proven themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be twenty-nine, probably married with a baby, and in a good job for four years. After that, I'd want a second string. A small business with my dad would be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take an embedded job, and save as much as I can. I'd marry in July, as planned. In the evenings I'd train as an electrician with my dad, so I have both skills when the robots reach hands-on work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. Five years lets us live a normal life while getting ready. I'd feel better if Lena's job held up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do family plans fit in the five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A baby by year three, if we can. We'd both work, and my mum would help with the child. I'd rather have a family before everything gets complicated, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use the tools at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use them for the boring parts: documentation, test cases, checking. But always check. I think that's how most people will do it in the end, so I'd rather copy what works than be first.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **prepare** if we're sensible.
I'd say to teach the young a **trade** as well as a degree.
think: I'd be twenty-nine, probably married with a baby, in a **good job** for four years.
I'd want a **second string**, like a small business with my dad.
do: Finish the master's, take an **embedded** job and save.
Train as an **electrician** with my dad in the evenings.
feel: I feel **uneasy, not scared**; five years lets us live a normal life.
S3.quote: I'd rather have a family before everything gets complicated, not after.
fieldNote: Jamal's answer to time is **family first** and a second skill.
He treats AI as a **tool for boring parts**, always checked.
Lena's **job security** is a key condition.

steps.text: Take the first embedded software job after the master's
Save as much of each pay as possible before the baby arrives
Train as an electrician with my dad in the evenings
Start a family by year three with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, and it's better to prepare than worry. I'd tell people at church to keep their families strong. And I'd say to the young that a trade and a degree together is a good bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be thirty-four, with two children, and possibly running part of my dad's firm. My engineering work might look different, but I'd have the skills to adapt. It feels like a normal life with some adjustment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take an embedded job, marry in July and save for a house. I'd learn the tools as they get proven, and I'd help my dad bring in more software at the firm. In five years, maybe buy a share of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade is enough for a normal life, children and a bit of change. I'd worry about my parents' retirement, but not about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your dad's firm over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's business, which supports them. If he retires in ten years and I'm running it, that helps everybody. If robots start doing electrical work by 2039, I'd want to be selling the service, not the labour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that stays steady for you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I'd rather keep my faith, my family and a good name. Those aren't things a machine can take, and they matter when the rest is changing.

I'd say a **trade and a degree** together is a good bet.
think: I'd be thirty-four with **two children**, possibly running part of my dad's firm.

Help my dad bring **software** into the firm.
Buy a **share** of the business in about five years.
feel: I feel **calm**; a decade is enough for a normal life.
S4.quote: If robots start doing electrical work by 2039, I'd want to be selling the service, not the labour.
fieldNote: Jamal is **calm** because the family firm gives a long runway.
He thinks about **ownership**, not just employment.
**Faith and family** are his fixed points.

steps.text: Work as an embedded engineer and help my dad modernise the firm
Save for a house deposit after the wedding
Buy a share of my dad's electrical firm within five years
Marry Lena in July and plan for two children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the wedding and the job would both be in the air and there's no time to get ready. What would help is my dad's firm still going, a fair chance at a first job and clear warnings from companies. I'd like our church community close by.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people forget graduates have lives too. I'm not just a CV. I've a fiancée, a family firm and a faith, and it's the ordinary things that keep me steady.

headlineQuote: I'm not just a CV. I've a fiancée, a family firm and a faith, and it's the ordinary things that keep me steady.
portrait: Jamal is a **24-year-old** embedded systems master's student in Augsburg who lives above his father's electrical firm.
He is **engaged to Lena**, a dental assistant, with a wedding in July and about thirteen thousand in loans.
His traditional, free-market views favour **work, trades and family**, and he treats AI as a checked helper.
He is steady: he waits for **proof**, then moves, and keeps his father's firm as a second path.
His mood runs from **uneasy** to anxious, and only a decade makes him calm.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because the wedding and his job search would both be uncertain at once.
whatWouldHelp: His **father's firm** still going, a fair chance at a first job and clear early warnings from companies.
